title: Buying Shoes for Children: Fit Before Everything
meta_description: How to measure a child's feet properly, how much growing room is safe, and which function shoes survive an evening of running on grass and marble.
keywords: kids shoes sizing guide, children khussa comfort, how to measure child foot, party shoes for kids Pakistan, growing room shoes
excerpt: Children's function shoes are bought for how they look and abandoned by hour two. Fit is the whole problem, and it is easy to get right.
imagePrompt: Three pairs of children's shoes arranged on cream linen — small embroidered gold khussas, closed velvet flats in deep plum, and simple leather party shoes in ivory — beside a paper foot-measuring template, a pencil and a folded pair of socks. Bright natural daylight, shallow depth of field, clean editorial flat-lay in warm neutrals, no faces, no text.

content.content:
Children's function shoes are bought the week of the event, chosen to match the outfit, tried on for thirty seconds in a shop, and worn for the first time at the function itself.

By the second hour they are off, and she is either barefoot on a marble floor or being carried.

The outfit gets weeks of thought and the shoes get ten minutes, which is the wrong way round — because at a function she will be running, standing, dancing and climbing, and the shoes are what decides whether she enjoys the evening.

Fit is nearly the whole problem, and fitting a child's foot properly takes about five minutes at home. Here is how, and what to buy once you know the size.

content.heading: Measure at Home, Properly
content.content:
Shop sizing varies enormously and a child cannot reliably tell you whether a shoe fits — young children will say yes to almost anything, and their toes curl rather than complain.

**Stand her on a sheet of paper** against a wall, with her weight on the foot. Feet spread when weight-bearing and a seated measurement is smaller than a standing one.

**Mark the longest toe** — which is not always the big toe — and the back of the heel.

**Measure both feet.** Most people have one longer foot, and you fit the larger one.

**Measure in the evening.** Feet are at their largest at the end of the day, which is when a function happens.

**Add a thumb's width of growing room**, roughly one centimetre, from the longest toe to the end of the shoe. Not more.

**Re-measure every two to three months** for children under about five. They grow through sizes far faster than clothes suggest, and a shoe that fitted at Eid may be too small by the winter.

content.heading: How Much Growing Room Is Safe
content.content:
The temptation is to buy large, because shoes are expensive and outgrown quickly. It is the wrong economy.

**One centimetre — about a thumb's width — is correct.** Enough for a few months of growth without affecting how she walks.

**Two sizes up is a genuine problem.** She will trip, she will scuff her toes, her heel will slip, and she will develop a shuffling walk to keep them on. At a function on a marble floor that is a fall waiting to happen.

**A slipping heel is the sign it is too big.** Hold the shoe on her foot and lift the heel — a little movement is fine, more than a centimetre is too much.

**Too small is worse than too big**, and it is harder to spot because children do not complain. Check by pressing at the toe with your thumb while she is standing.

**Do not judge by the size on the previous pair.** Sizing differs between makers by as much as a full size, so measure and check every time rather than ordering by number.

content.heading: Khussas and Traditional Flats
content.content:
The traditional choice, and correct for many functions — with two things to know before buying.

**Leather khussas are stiff when new.** They need breaking in over several evenings at home. A new pair worn straight to a wedding is why children end up barefoot.

**They run narrow with almost no give across the width.** A child with a wide foot may need a size up for width, which then makes them too long — in that case, look for a different style rather than compromising.

**The flat sole has no cushioning.** Fine for two hours, hard going for five on a hard floor. A thin padded insole added inside makes a real difference and costs almost nothing.

**They slip on and off easily**, which is a genuine advantage at a home function or a mosque where shoes come off at the door.

**Embroidered khussas crush.** Pack them separately and never under anything heavy — our [packing guide](/journal/packing-formal-wear-travel-without-creasing) covers travelling with formal wear.

**Kolhapuris and soft embroidered mules** work similarly and are often more comfortable straight from the box.

content.heading: Matching the Shoe to the Venue
content.content:
The venue should decide the shoe, exactly as it does for adults.

**A lawn or garden.** Grass is uneven and, in winter, damp. Flats or a low block heel for an older girl. Fabric and suede shoes will mark; leather or a coated finish survives.

**A marquee.** Carpet over uneven ground. Flats.

**A hall or hotel.** Hard polished floors, which are slippery. Check the sole has some grip — a new leather sole on marble is genuinely slippery, and scuffing it with sandpaper before the day helps.

**A home function.** Shoes come off at the door. Choose something she can remove and put back on herself without help, because she will do it several times.

**Winter, anywhere.** Closed shoes with warm socks. Cold feet on grass or marble at eleven o'clock end a child's evening faster than anything else. Our post on [dressing children for winter weddings](/journal/kids-winter-wedding-outfits-pakistan) covers the rest of the outfit.

**Summer, anywhere.** Open or breathable, and expect feet to swell in heat.

content.heading: What to Look For in the Shoe Itself
content.content:
**A flexible sole that bends at the ball of the foot**, not in the middle. A stiff sole that will not bend forces an unnatural walk.

**A firm heel cup.** Press the back of the shoe between finger and thumb — it should hold its shape rather than collapsing. This is what keeps the foot stable.

**A fastening that holds.** A strap, a buckle or elastic. A shoe held on by nothing but friction comes off while running.

**A fastening she can manage herself.** Velcro or elastic for younger children; buckles are fine from about six or seven. This matters more than it sounds at a function where shoes come off at the door.

**Breathable lining.** Plastic linings make feet sweat, and a sweaty foot in a smooth shoe slides and blisters.

**Light weight.** Heavy party shoes are tiring on a small child across a long evening.

**Check the inside with your hand** for seams, stitching ends and glue ridges — the same check as for a garment lining. Our [quality checklist](/journal/quality-kids-festive-outfit-mothers-buying-checklist) covers the same approach for clothing.

content.heading: Breaking Them In
content.content:
The single most useful thing on this page, and it takes almost no effort.

**Two or three evenings at home** in the shoes, an hour at a time, on a hard floor. This is enough for most shoes.

**With the socks she will wear.** Sock thickness changes the fit meaningfully, and a shoe fitted barefoot can be tight over a winter sock.

**Watch for redness after wearing.** Marks on the heel, the little toe or the top of the foot show where a shoe will rub for four hours.

**Deal with a rub before the day.** A blister plaster applied preventatively works far better than one applied after.

**Do not buy the week of the function** if you can avoid it. Two weeks gives time to break them in and to exchange them if they turn out wrong.

**Keep one comfortable, broken-in pair** that works across several functions rather than buying a new pair for each. A neutral gold or ivory flat goes with almost every outfit and saves both money and blisters. Our post on [kids' formals that last more than one season](/journal/kids-formal-wear-that-lasts-more-than-one-season) makes the same argument for clothing.

content.heading: On the Day
content.content:
**Pack a spare pair of socks.** Grass is damp at winter functions and wet socks are the fastest route to a miserable child.

**Bring a comfortable backup pair.** Simple flats or sandals in the bag. She will want them by hour three, and having her own beats borrowing.

**Label them at a home function.** Twenty pairs of small khussas by a door look remarkably similar at midnight, and losing one shoe is worse than losing both.

**Bring a small bag for them** if shoes come off at the door and are likely to disappear.

**Blister plasters in your bag**, which cost nothing and save an evening.

**Check her feet at some point.** Children will keep running in shoes that are hurting rather than stop and say so.

**Let her be barefoot if she wants to be** at a home function. It is warm, the floor is clean, and it is not worth a fight. Our post on [dressing children for a dholki](/journal/how-to-dress-kids-pakistani-dholki-night) covers the informal end, where shoes barely feature at all. questions.question: How do I measure a child's foot at home?
questions.answer: Stand her on paper against a wall with her weight on the foot, mark the longest toe and the back of the heel, and measure both feet — most people have one longer. Do it in the evening, when feet are at their largest, and re-measure every two to three months.

questions.question: How much growing room should children's shoes have?
questions.answer: About one centimetre — a thumb's width — from the longest toe to the end of the shoe. Two sizes up is a genuine problem: she will trip, the heel will slip, and she will develop a shuffling walk to keep them on, which is dangerous on a polished floor.

questions.question: Are khussas comfortable for children at a wedding?
questions.answer: They can be, but not new. Leather khussas are stiff and need breaking in over several evenings, they run narrow with little give, and the flat sole has no cushioning. A thin padded insole added inside makes a real difference across a long evening.

questions.question: What should I check when buying children's party shoes?
questions.answer: A sole that bends at the ball of the foot rather than the middle, a firm heel cup that holds its shape when pressed, a fastening that holds and that she can manage herself, breathable lining, and light weight. Run your hand inside for seams and glue ridges.

questions.question: How long does it take to break in children's shoes?
questions.answer: Two or three evenings at home, an hour at a time on a hard floor, wearing the socks she will actually wear — sock thickness changes the fit meaningfully. Watch for redness afterwards, which shows where a shoe will rub for four hours at the function.
